title: Basic Evaluate Call
background:
Most application code uses JsonE.Net through a single method call: `JsonE.Evaluate(template, context)`. You provide the template as a `JsonNode` and the context as another JSON value, and the library returns the evaluated output as `JsonNode?`.

This lesson focuses on wiring that call correctly. The objective is not to design template syntax, but to execute an evaluation from C# and return the library result unchanged.
instructions: Call `JsonE.Evaluate(template, context)` and return the result.

title: Context Fallback
background:
In production code, input data may not always include a usable context object. JsonE.Net accepts an empty object context, so a common integration pattern is to normalize a missing or null context to `new JsonObject()` before evaluating.

This keeps your wrapper predictable and avoids propagating input-shape assumptions throughout your app. The lesson focuses on context preparation in C#, not template design.
instructions: Use an empty `JsonObject` when `test["context"]` is null, then evaluate the template.

title: Built-in Function Invocation
background:
JsonE.Net exposes built-in functions through expression evaluation. From C#, you invoke them by passing a template expression to `JsonE.Evaluate`, then supplying the required symbols in context.

This lesson practices constructing an expression string for a built-in function call. The library skill is building the template input for evaluation, then returning the evaluated `JsonNode`.
instructions: Set the `$eval` expression to call `max(x, y)` and return the evaluated result.

title: Custom Function Registration
background:
When built-ins are not enough, JsonE.Net lets you register custom functions by adding `JsonFunction` values to the context object. The function can then be called from expressions evaluated by `JsonE.Evaluate`.

This lesson focuses on adding a function to context before evaluation. You are exercising the `JsonFunction.Create(...)` extension point from C# code.
instructions: Add a `mod` function to the context using `JsonFunction.Create`, then evaluate the template.

title: Custom Function Argument Validation
background:
Custom functions receive `JsonNode?[]` parameters. In application code, you should validate argument count and types before performing numeric or string operations, so your function fails predictably.

This lesson focuses on defensive function design. You will return `null` for invalid input instead of throwing, and otherwise return a computed JSON value.
instructions: Create a `safeDiv` custom function that returns `null` for invalid input or division by zero, otherwise `x / y`.

title: EvaluationContext Access
background:
JsonE.Net passes an `EvaluationContext` into custom functions. This lets a function inspect currently available symbols without hard-coding every value into its argument list.

In this lesson, you will use context-aware behavior through `IsDefined(...)`. The goal is to practice the library extension point, not to teach template operators.
instructions: Add a `hasSymbol(name)` custom function that returns whether a context symbol is defined using `EvaluationContext`.

title: Deterministic Time Context
background:
Some JsonE evaluations depend on current time. In app code and tests, deterministic behavior is important, so a common approach is to inject a fixed `now` value into context before calling `JsonE.Evaluate`.

This lesson practices controlling time-sensitive behavior at the library integration layer. You will add `now` only when it is missing.
instructions: If `now` is missing from context, add it from `test["now"]` before evaluation.

title: Reusable Evaluation Method
background:
Applications often centralize JsonE evaluation behind a small helper method so context normalization and invocation rules are in one place. This keeps call sites simple and consistent.

This lesson focuses on implementing that helper pattern in C#. You will call a private method that wraps `JsonE.Evaluate`.
instructions: Implement `EvaluateTemplate` so it normalizes null context to an empty object, then use it from `Run`.

title: JsonEException Catch Pattern
background:
Runtime evaluation can fail for several reasons. At integration points, the most practical baseline is to catch `JsonEException` and return a controlled diagnostic value instead of propagating failures directly to UI code.

This lesson focuses on implementing that catch pattern. It gives you a stable library-facing error boundary for calling `JsonE.Evaluate`.
instructions: Wrap evaluation in `try/catch (JsonEException)` and return the exception type name when evaluation fails.

title: Exception Type Mapping
background:
Sometimes applications need simplified error categories instead of raw exception type names. You can catch `JsonEException` and map known subtypes to stable labels for telemetry or UI messaging.

This lesson focuses on subtype mapping logic around JsonE.Net exceptions. The key skill is handling library exceptions consistently in C# code.
instructions: Catch `JsonEException` and map subtypes to these strings: `template`, `interpreter`, `builtin`, `syntax`, otherwise `unknown`.
